I obtained my Bachelor’s degree in Economics and Finance from University of Hong Kong in 2019, and Master of Arts in Economics from Duke University in 2021. I was a visiting scholar at MIT Department of Economics from 2024-2025. Prior to academia, I worked as an analyst at Softbank Venture Capital.
I grew up in Hunan province in mainland China where we are known for our spicy-eating culture.

title: Propagation of Industrial Policy Along Supply Chains: Evidence from Government Venture Capital in China
text: This paper focuses on the context of China and examines the allocation and effects on aggregate TFP of Government Venture Capital (Government VC) using linked firm-level and supply-chain data. I find that in China, Government VC accounts for approximately 10% of the venture capital market and targets strategic sectors, including semiconductors, with high Domar weights, substantial import dependence, and scope for innovation and learning by doing. Within sectors, Government VC-backed firms together with their suppliers and buyers have broader buyer networks and higher innovation intensity than firms without VC backing or those backed by private VC. To understand the firm-level effect of Government VC investment, I adopted a staggered difference-in-differences design, and I find that Government VC increases funded firms’ sales by 14.5%, wage bill by 12.8%, and capital by 15.1% on average within 2 years. The effects spread through production networks: suppliers’ sales increase by 2.5%, wage bill increases by 2.7%, capital increases by 1.5% on average within 2 years, and buyers’ sales increase by 4.1%, wage bill increases by 3.6%, capital increases by 1.2% on average within 2 years. These patterns are consistent with propagation through supply and demand linkages. Aggregating the estimated effects in a Baqaee–Farhi production-network framework, I find that Government VC raises manufacturing aggregate TFP by 0.07%, equivalent to approximately RMB 14.51 billion in the 2016 benchmark economy, driven by factor reallocation. As a case of discretionary industrial policy, Government VC demonstrates how targeting improves aggregate efficiency through improving resource allocation efficiency in the short run.

Coordination in Production Networks
text: Using Chinese VAT administrative data, I study complementarities when upstream and downstream firms receive investment simultaneously. I examine how information frictions, financing constraints, and decentralized decision-making generate under-coordination, and whether government coordination and policy intervention can internalize production-network complementarities.

title: Are Banks Discriminatory? Evidence from U.S. Residential Lending
text: We merge court-order data with bank Call Reports to construct a matched panel of more than two million observations and use a difference-in-differences (DiD) design to identify the causal effects of judicial interventions on lending behavior and bank credit-supply elasticity.

title: Exchange-Rate Movements and U.S. Corporations
text:
Abstract
Use U.S. Census LFTTD microdata and shift-share instruments to estimate the effects of exchange-rate exposure and the associated elasticities for exports, sales, and equity returns. The study provides firm-level micro evidence showing that the apparent macro-level exchange rate-stock market disconnect does not hold.

title: Research
text:
Using linked firm and supply-chain data from China, this paper examines where government venture capital (Government VC) invests and how its effects spread through production networks. Government VC targets strategic, import-dependent sectors, and within sector, it targets at innovative, high capital revenue productivity firms. Within two years of investment, backed firms’ sales rise by 14.5%, with gains extending to suppliers and buyers. A production-network model implies that government VC raises manufacturing TFP by 0.07%, mainly through factor reallocation.
